“Mutius … is coming tomorrow for a few days.”

Mutius is also discussed at length in Schmitt’s letters to N. Sombart, who had known him since the early 1930s and later became his colleague and friend at the Council of Europe in Strasbourg. In 1979 Sombart delivered the funeral address for him; typescript in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 21820.

Nicolaus asked about the patriot — See Nicolaus Sombart, “Patriotismus im Welt-Bürgerkrieg.” In: Der Zeitgenosse und sein Vaterland. Eine Vortragsreihe des Bayerischen Rundfunks. Edited by Gerhard Szczesny, Munich 1957, pp. 31–51.
I answered him — Letter of 3 February 1957 (BW Sombart, pp. 96 ff.).
“Those were never your bells …” — From the poem “Venus Religio” by Richard Dehmel (1863–1920), in: R. Dehmel, Die Verwandlung der Venus, Berlin 1907, p. 59.
Peter Schneider’s book — See the note above on p. 329.
πολλὰ τὰ δεινά — πολλὰ τὰ δεινά κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει.
“Many powerful things exist, but nothing is more powerful than man.”
Meanwhile Hans Zehrer is trumpeting … — H. Zehrer, “Wer hat die Macht?” In: Die Welt, 30 March 1957.
killing of Wallenstein in 1634 (according to Pekař) — Josef Pekař, Wallenstein 1630–1634. Tragödie einer Verschwörung, Berlin 1937.
“Even the murder of the monarch …” — Quoted in abbreviated form. Kant writes:

“Among all the horrors of a revolution brought about by rebellion, even the murder of the monarch is not the worst. For one can still imagine that the people kill him out of fear that, if he remains alive, he may recover his power and make them suffer the punishment they deserve. In that case it would not be an act of punitive justice, but merely one of self-preservation. It is the formal execution that fills a soul steeped in the idea of human rights with a horror that is felt again and again whenever one thinks of such a scene, as in the fate of Charles I or Louis XVI. […] But how are we to explain this feeling, which is not aesthetic […] but moral—a feeling produced by the complete reversal of every concept of law? It is regarded as a crime that remains forever and can never be erased (crimen immortale, inexpiabile)…”
Kant, Werke in zehn Bänden. Edited by Wilhelm Weischedel, vol. 7, Darmstadt 1968, pp. 440 f.
my expert opinion on the scelus infandum — This refers to Angriffskrieg, p. 16; see also the notes above on pp. 66 and 219.
The land of socialist construction — Correctly:

“By contrast, the land of socialist construction has committed all its enormous power to ensuring—and must unfailingly use it to ensure—that power over human beings comes to an end. […] So that instead of the so-called constitutional state, which because of its rotten class content has become completely a state of injustice, no state at all will any longer be necessary.”
Ernst Bloch, Das Prinzip Hoffnung, Frankfurt am Main 1959, p. 1061.

Tantam fidem non inveni nisi in Israel! — Correctly: audiens autem Iesus miratus est et sequentibus se dixit amen dico vobis non inveni tantam fidem in Israel; Vulgate, Matthew 8:10. Luther translates:
“When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him: Truly I tell you, I have found no such faith in anyone in Israel.”
Tantam justificationem per finem non inveni apud Jesuitas! — Schmitt’s alteration of the preceding quotation:
“Such a justification by the final goal I have not found even among the Jesuits.”
“Why do you beat your breast and groan? Why do you shed useless tears and refuse to admit that you willingly obey criminal orders?”
trahimur sub nomine pacis — “Peace is being used as a pretext to enslave us.” Pharsalia, IV, 222.

Dachau Trial, April/May 1957 — In the issue mentioned, Der Spiegel, under the title “Der Furcht so fern, dem Tod so nah,” reports on the 1957 proceedings before the Munich jury court and the Osnabrück Regional Court against the SS leaders Dietrich, Lippert, von Woyrsch, and Müller-Altenau for their participation in the Röhm murders. The article emphasizes the Reichswehr’s interest in eliminating the SA.

Potempa Trial — During the night of 9–10 August 1932, SA men murdered the worker Konrad Pietrzuch in the Silesian village of Potempa. On the same day, 9 August, the Reich government had issued an emergency decree against political terrorism providing for the death penalty. As a result, the five murderers were sentenced to death in a rapid trial on 22 August.

A large National Socialist propaganda campaign against the “blood verdict” followed, after which the Reich President felt compelled to commute the death sentences to life imprisonment. After the Nazi seizure of power, the perpetrators were released in March 1933.

Robert Graves — Schmitt is referring to Graves’s edition of Lucan: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, Pharsalia. Dramatic Episodes of the Civil Wars. Translated by Robert Graves (The Penguin Classics, 66), Harmondsworth 1956. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 23823.
He is rhetorical; Th. Hobbes already knew that — The reference to Hobbes concerns his comment in the preface to his translation of the Odyssey:

“Lucan shews himself openly in the Pompeyan Faction, inveighing against Caesar throughout his Poem, like Cicero against Cataline [sic!] or Marc Antony, and is therefore justly reckon’d by Quintilian as a Rhetorician rather than a Poet.”

Quoted from “Preface to Homer’s Odysses, translated by Tho. Hobbes of Malmsbury.” In: Critical Essays of the Seventeenth Century, ed. J. E. Spingarn, vol. II, 1650–1685, Oxford 1908, p. 73. See also David Norbrook, Writing the English Republic. Poetry, Rhetoric and Politics 1627–1660, Cambridge 2000, chapter 1, “Lucan and the Poetry of Civil War,” pp. 23–62.
si scelus est plus te nobis debere fatere … — Correctly:
Si scelus est, plus te nobis debere fateris, / Quod scelus hoc non ipse facis.
“If it is a crime, you admit that you owe us all the more because you are not committing this crime yourself.”
essay whose boldness—indeed, audacity—no one understood at the time — See Wolfgang Schuller’s afterword in Tb 1930–34, pp. 461 ff.
press chief Du Prel — Maximilian Du Prel (1904–1945), jurist and National Socialist politician, was in 1934 “Reich Office Director of the NSDAP Reich Press Office.”

Funck-Brentano — Frantz Funck-Brentano (1862–1947), French writer and historian. The work mentioned, however, appeared not in 1907 but in 1912: F. Funck-Brentano, L’ancienne France. Le roi, Paris 1912.

Roegele — Otto B. Roegele (1920–2005), editor-in-chief of the Rheinischer Merkur, its publisher from 1963 onward, and professor of newspaper studies in Munich. Schmitt’s two-page letter to Warnach was written on 29 May 1957. Published in Vorber.
Calvo Serer — Rafael Calvo Serer (1916–1988), Spanish philosopher of history, invited Schmitt to Spain during the 1950s.
I wrote to Peter Schneider — Letter in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 13493.
What am I still doing in this world? / Do you see the lightning falling there? — Quotation from the poem “Das Gewitter” by Gustav Benjamin Schwab (1792–1850).

conversation with George Schwab — G. D. Schwab (born 1931), American political scientist and translator of Schmitt. His doctorate at Columbia University in New York was initially blocked in 1962 by Otto Kirchheimer’s vote and could only proceed after Kirchheimer’s death in 1965. The dissertation appeared in 1970 as G. Schwab, The Challenge of the Exception. An Introduction to the Political Ideas of Carl Schmitt Between 1921–1936, Berlin 1970. During the 1950s, Schwab visited Schmitt several times.
we laughed at Adorno’s revealing remark — Hegel’s thought contained:
“something of the grand peasant cunning that has learned for so long to bow before the powerful and adapt itself to their needs that it can finally wrest power away from them.”
T. W. Adorno, Drei Studien zu Hegel. In: idem, Gesammelte Schriften. Edited by Rolf Tiedemann, vol. 5, 3rd ed., Frankfurt am Main 1990, p. 287.

Wonderful, by contrast, was Hans Freyer in his reply to Arnold Gehlen’s birthday speech — Gehlen described the birthday celebration and his disagreement with Schmitt in a letter to Helmut Schelsky dated 3 August 1957:

“Freyer’s birthday was pleasant; honorary doctorate from Münster. The Grand Cross of Merit will probably follow. My lecture—the thesis was that Freyer had shown, though without explicitly saying so, that in the future history would cease to provide the interpretation of the present and sociology would take its place—was well received, but not by C. S., who has now, of all things, discovered HEGEL and wants to impose him on everyone. He got terribly on my nerves. I found him more venomous, resentful, and arrogant than ever before, constantly forcing his ‘discoveries’ on everyone. Even Hamlet was really nothing more than an inflated trifle.”
University and State Library Münster, Papers of Schelsky, box 23, 030.

Papalekas — Johannes Chr. Papalekas (1924–1996), sociologist, then working at the Social Research Center in Dortmund. He completed his postdoctoral qualification under Hans Freyer and later became professor in Münster and Bochum. Schmitt met him at the time of Kojève’s lecture in Düsseldorf in January 1957; see his letter to Sombart of 3 February 1957 (BW Sombart, pp. 96 ff.).
Ubi nihil vales … — See the note above on p. 14.

As Michel Mourre did then in Notre Dame — At Easter 1950, Mourre, wearing a Dominican habit, climbed into the pulpit of Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris during Mass and announced to the congregation: “God is dead.” See his autobiography Malgré le blasphème, Paris 1951; German: Gott ist tot, Vienna/Munich 1954; BW Mohler, p. 181 and passim.

Georg Lukács in the same tragicomic situation — Lukács served in 1956 as Minister of Education in Imre Nagy’s government and was arrested after the suppression of the Budapest uprising. From then on he was under official disgrace.
the note at the end of my expert opinion — Angriffskrieg, pp. 80 f.
precedent — An allusion to Anglo-American case law.
Hugo Ball criticized my Political Romanticism … — Hugo Ball, “Carl Schmitts Politische Theologie.” In: Hochland 21, 1924, p. 466.
Three grim prophecies — Based on an epigram by Schiller and Goethe:
In vain, Germans, you hope to shape yourselves into a nation; Instead, if you can, shape yourselves more freely into human beings.
Friedrich Schiller, Sämtliche Werke in 5 Bänden. Edited by P.-A. Alt, A. Meier, and W. Riedel, vol. 1, Munich 2004, p. 267.
that I spoke of the “proletarian consciousness of having been cheated” — Possibly a reference to PuB, pp. 129 f.:

“The fascist ethos, too, proceeds from that feeling of having been cheated which can be found everywhere from the nineteenth century onward, which is by no means merely a proletarian emotion, and which after the World War found stronger expression in the Latin countries than in Germany.”
Bloch’s remarks have not been identified.

So good old Werner Becker expects … — W. Becker (1904–1981), jurist and theologian, a student of Schmitt in Bonn who earned his doctorate under him with a dissertation on Hobbes; see W. Becker, Briefe an Carl Schmitt. Edited and annotated by Piet Tommissen, Berlin 1998, pp. 10 ff.
Schmitt is probably referring to W. Becker, Die Wirklichkeit der Kirche und das Ärgernis, Leipzig 1957. Two copies are in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 nos. 26637 and 26681.
pecca fortiter — Luther wrote to Melanchthon on 1 August 1521:
Esto peccator et pecca fortiter, sed fortius fide et gaude in Christo, qui victor est peccati, mortis et mundi.
“Be a sinner and sin boldly, but be still stronger in faith and in your joy in Christ, who is the victor over sin, death, and the world.”
M. Luther, D. Martin Luthers Werke (Weimar edition), section 4, vol. 2, p. 372.
Et ta Race est 89 — The French “Jacobin” historian Jules Michelet (1798–1874) wrote:
“From India down to ’89 there flows a torrent of light, the river of Right and Reason. You are high antiquity. And your race is ’89.”
J. Michelet, Bible de l’humanité, Paris 1864, p. 485.
Aubrey Beardsley seems to have been right — Schmitt is referring here to Franz Blei, who described an encounter with Beardsley and quoted him as saying:
“Every one of us. Nothing but Hamlets. The Protestant ending.”
F. Blei, Zeitgenössische Bildnisse, Amsterdam 1940, p. 194.

trial of Böhme — In the 1958 “Ulm Einsatzgruppen Trial,” former SS Sturmbannführer Hans-Joachim Böhme (1909–1960), together with other defendants, was sentenced to fifteen years in prison for assisting in 3,907 instances of collective murder committed in Lithuania in 1941.
Pflimlin — Pierre Eugène Jean Pflimlin (1907–2000), French jurist and politician, briefly Prime Minister of France in 1958.
Kühlmann — Richard von Kühlmann (1873–1948), German diplomat and industrialist, State Secretary of the Foreign Office from 1917 to 1918.
par nobile fratrum — “A noble pair of brothers,” used ironically to mean “a fine pair indeed”; quotation from the satires of Horace.
C. F. von Weizsäcker’s account — Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, Die gegenwärtigen Aussichten einer Begrenzung der Gefahr eines Atomkrieges, Hamburg 1958.

Poor Delano — In Herman Melville’s story Benito Cereno, the American captain Amasa Delano visits a Spanish slave ship lying at anchor without realizing that its captain, Benito Cereno, is being held hostage by the slaves who have mutinied.
who therefore calls himself Carlo — An allusion to Carlo Schmid, with whom Schmitt was occasionally confused and who was still calling himself “Karl” in 1948; see the note above on p. 52.
Otto Weininger’s hatred of the Viennese waltz — See O. Weininger, Über die letzten Dinge, 4th ed., Vienna/Leipzig 1918, p. 99. See also the note above on p. 253.

a pension under Article 131 — Article 131 of the Basic Law provided that the pension and employment status of civil servants who were not reinstated after 1945 was to be regulated by federal law. This was done on 11 May 1951 in such a way that everyone who had not been classified as a major offender or offender could once again be employed as a civil servant or become eligible for a pension. Schmitt thereby became entitled to receive his pension.
July 1958, Christian Courtois’s book — Chr. Courtois, Les Vandales et l’Afrique, Paris 1955.

Gelimer’s laughter and Daniel’s smile — On Gelimer, see above, p. 312. For Schmitt, Gelimer’s opposite was the Romanesque statue at the portal of Santiago Cathedral showing the prophet Daniel laughing over the lions that could do him no harm. See BW Forsthoff, pp. 161 f., 540 (illustration); BW d’Ors, p. 191; Schmittiana NF I, 2011, p. 243.
